We can learn from the mistakes of the past, strengthen our resolve, and implement a prohibition policy that is more effective and sustainable.

Reinstating national prohibition is not a panacea, and it will undoubtedly face challenges. Title: Reinstating National Prohibition: A Responsible Step Towards Public Health and Moral Values

Introduction

The issue of prohibitions and regulations regarding the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in the United States has been a contentious subject throughout history. The Twenty-first Amendment, passed in 1933, officially ended the nationwide prohibition of alcohol. However, some believe that a modern form of prohibition would align better with the interests of societal well-being and moral rectitude. This essay stands in favor of reintroducing a national prohibition on alcoholic beverages, juxtaposing its potential benefits against the detrimental impact of alcohol consumption on public health, safety, and moral values.

Public Health Implications

Each year, alcohol-related harm contributes to countless preventable deaths, injuries, illnesses, and financial burdens. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), excessive alcohol use is the fourth leading cause of death in the US, accounting for over 95,000 deaths annually. Further, alcohol-impaired driving causes thousands of deaths and injuries each year, often involving innocent bystanders. Statistics reveal that one in six reported motor vehicle crash deaths involve an alcohol-impaired driver. These grim realities emphasize the urgent need to curb alcohol-related harm in our communities.

The financial cost to society is staggering. Direct medical costs attributed to alcohol amount to approximately $24.7 billion annually. Indirect costs, including lost productivity due to alcohol-related absenteeism and decreased workplace performance, further exacerbate this burden. Moreover, families and communities pay a heavy price in terms of emotional and psychological trauma caused by alcohol use disorders, domestic violence, child abuse, and neglect. By reinstating national prohibition, we assert our commitment to safeguarding public health and minimizing these unnecessary expenses.

Moral Imperative

Inextricably linked to the issue of public health are moral concerns. Numerous studies have demonstrated that consuming alcohol impairs judgment and self-control, thus compromising an individual's ability to act responsibly and empathize with others. When under the influence, people are more likely to engage in antisocial behavior, exhibit aggression, and commit violence. In this sense, alcohol consumption directly contradicts many of the moral virtues foundational to a strong and cohesive society, such as empathy, respect, and personal accountability.

Another moral consideration is the detrimental impact of alcohol on vulnerable populations, including minors and pregnant women. Alcohol use during pregnancy can cause irreversible fetal damage, leading to a range of lifelong physical, cognitive, and behavioral problems in children. Consequently, enforcing a national prohibition may protect these at-risk groups from potential harm and uphold a moral duty of care we owe them.

Societal Harmony and Progress

Prohibition is not a novel concept and has been implemented in various forms across human history. While the well-intended and universally lauded Eighteenth Amendment eventually fell short of its goal due to widespread corruption, adverse economic consequences, and violent black markets, recent research suggests that reversing the decision could afford us the opportunity to address present-day challenges posed by alcohol in an informed and measured manner.

Modern knowledge and research in fields such as addiction psychology, epidemiology, and public health policy provide us with the tools and insights necessary to create a more nuanced and effective national prohibition framework. This might involve strict penalties for those who flout the law, as well as comprehensive preventative measures targeting various aspects of society, such as education programs, support networks for those suffering from alcohol use disorders, and evidence-based interventions aimed at minimizing harm to individuals and communities.

Conclusion

While national prohibition is not a perfect solution to the pervasive problem of alcohol misuse, reestablishing a nationwide ban on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages would be a significant step towards enhancing public health, fostering moral values, and promoting societal harmony and progress. In an age where our knowledge and understanding of addiction, public health, and social issues have advanced considerably since the last attempt at prohibition, it is incumbent upon us to take stock of current evidence and make informed decisions that will best serve the interests of all Americans. As such, reinstating national prohibition is a responsible course of action worth considering and advocating for.

The Case for National Temperance: Reinstate Prohibition to Save America

Introduction

In the heart of every great nation lies the moral fiber that binds its citizens together, fostering health, prosperity, and unity. Yet, one of the most insidious threats to this fabric is the legalized sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages. Since the repeal of Prohibition in 1933, alcohol has wreaked havoc on American society, contributing to millions of deaths, shattered families, and crippling healthcare systems. It is time to acknowledge the undeniable truth: the reinstatement of a national prohibition on alcohol is not only a public health imperative but a moral necessity for the United States. History has demonstrated that when we prioritize virtue over vice, society flourishes. From the abolition of slavery to the prohibition of child labor, America has repeatedly proven that strong moral leadership can elevate the nation. Just as we once recognized the dangers of unchecked alcohol consumption and took bold action, we must do so again—this time with greater understanding, technological advancement, and unwavering resolve.

The Devastating Public Health Crisis of Alcohol

Alcohol is one of the most dangerous and widely used legal substances in the United States, responsible for nearly 95,000 deaths annually and costing the nation $249 billion per year in healthcare expenses, lost productivity, and crime-related costs (CDC, 2023). Unlike many other health threats, alcohol’s harm is not confined to heavy drinkers; its effects ripple through families, workplaces, and entire communities. The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen, directly linked to cancers of the mouth, throat, liver, and breast. Yet, despite these well-documented dangers, alcohol remains glorified in media, industry lobbying prevents stricter regulations, and generations of Americans have been conditioned to accept drink as a normal part of life—despite its proven lethality.

The direct health impacts of alcohol are staggering:

  • Liver disease: Alcoholic liver disease is the second-leading cause of liver cirrhosis deaths in the U.S., with over 30,000 deaths annually attributed to alcohol-related liver conditions.
  • Cardiovascular disease: Even moderate drinking increases the risk of hypertension, stroke, and heart failure.
  • Mental health crises: Alcohol is a depressant that exacerbates anxiety, depression, and suicide. Studies show that 30% of suicides are alcohol-related.
  • Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD): Every year, thousands of babies are born with lifelong disabilities due to prenatal alcohol exposure, a tragedy entirely preventable through abstinence.

Beyond individual health, alcohol fuels a public health emergency through its role in accidents, violence, and crime. Drunk driving alone kills more than 10,000 Americans annually, while alcohol is a factor in nearly half of all violent crimes, including domestic abuse and sexual assault. The economic burden is equally crippling—binge drinking costs society $191 billion per year in lost productivity, healthcare, and criminal justice expenses (NIH, 2022). If a foreign disease or virus were causing this level of devastation, the government would declare a national emergency. Yet, because alcohol is a legally entrenched industry, we accept this suffering as an unavoidable "cost of civilization."

The tobacco control movement offers a powerful precedent. In the 1960s, smoking was socially acceptable, heavily marketed, and even endorsed by doctors. Today, thanks to public health campaigns and regulation, smoking rates have plummeted by over 60% since 1965. The same approach must be taken with alcohol—not through weak "responsible drinking" messages, but through outright prohibition of production, sale, and public consumption.

Alcohol and the Collapse of the American Family

The true cost of alcohol is measured not in dollars, but in shattered lives, broken homes, and lost futures. Over 1 in 3 children in the U.S. report having lived with someone who was an alcoholic, and 1 in 5 adults grew up in a household with alcohol abuse (SAMHSA, 2021). The consequences are dire:

  • Child neglect and abuse: Alcohol impairs judgment and increases aggression. Children of alcoholics are three to four times more likely to suffer neglect or abuse.
  • Domestic violence: Studies show that 50% of intimate partner homicides involve alcohol intoxication.
  • Economic instability: Families struggle under the financial strain of alcoholism, with many forgoing basic needs—food, healthcare, education—to sustain their addiction.

The moral argument for prohibition is strongest when we consider its role in eroding the foundation of society: the family. When a substance destroys marriages, leaves children orphaned by addiction, and turns breadwinners into burdens on social services, it is no longer a matter of personal choice—it is a public evil. Parents have a moral duty to protect their children, and society has a duty to protect its future generations. Allowing alcohol to remain legal is like permitting a poison to be sold in grocery stores—knowing that it will harm the most vulnerable among us.

Historically, societies that tolerated widespread drunkenness saw cultural decline and moral decay. Ancient Rome’s fall has been partly attributed to alcohol abuse among its elite; medieval Europe witnessed periods of reformation where temperance movements flourished to combat societal breakdown. America in the 21st century faces the same crisis: a nation that claims to value family, discipline, and virtue is slowly being undermined by a legalized vice that tears those values apart.

The Moral Imperative: Reclaiming Virtue in a Drunken Society

Beyond the measurable harms, alcohol represents a fundamental moral failure in American culture. Critics may argue that prohibition is "paternalistic" or "authoritarian," but history shows that governments have always regulated substances harmful to the public good. We ban heroin, cocaine, and methamphetamine—not because their users are criminals, but because they destroy lives and society. Alcohol does the same, yet it is treated with far more leniency.

Consider the Christian principle of sobriety—alcohol is condemned in Scripture as a "mocker" and a "brawler" (Proverbs 20:1), something that leads to folly rather than wisdom. Many religious traditions, from Islam to evangelical Christianity to certain forms of Judaism, prohibit alcohol entirely on moral grounds. Even secular ethical frameworks, such as utilitarianism, would demand prohibition if the alternative is widespread addiction, suffering, and death.

The moral case can be summed up in three key points:

  1. Alcohol is a Tool of Oppression – It preys on the weak, trapping them in cycles of dependency while enriching corporate interests. The alcohol industry spends over $3 billion annually on advertising, specifically targeting youth, minorities, and low-income communities—those most vulnerable to addiction.
  2. It Corrupts Civic Virtue – A nation of sober, disciplined citizens is a nation capable of greatness. Alcohol weakens self-control, fuels domestic strife, and distracts from higher pursuits of art, science, and civic duty.
  3. Prohibition is a Test of Social Commitment – Just as we ban drunk driving despite its challenges, we must extend that logic to all alcohol use. If we truly believe in life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, we must recognize that alcohol is a false happiness—a temporary escape that ultimately destroys real joy.

Some will argue that personal freedom outweighs moral concerns, but freedom without responsibility is license, not liberty. True freedom comes from self-mastery—from the ability to resist base impulses that harm ourselves and others. Far from being oppressive, prohibition would liberate millions from addiction, poverty, and societal decay.

Addressing the Counterarguments: Why Economic and Libertarian Concerns Falter

Opponents of prohibition typically raise three major objections:

  1. "It will destroy jobs and the economy."
  2. "Adults should have the right to choose what they consume."
  3. "Prohibition failed in the 1920s—black markets and crime will return."

These objections, while understandable, are fundamentally flawed when weighed against the overwhelming evidence of alcohol’s harm.

1. The Alcoholic Beverage Industry is a Harmful Parasite

The alcohol industry generates $273 billion in annual revenue and employs millions of Americans. However, this economic benefit is a false economy—a superficial gain that masks the trillions in healthcare costs, lost productivity, and suffering caused by alcohol.

  • Comparison with Tobacco: The tobacco industry once argued that banning cigarettes would devastate the economy. Instead, smart regulation, high taxes, and consumer education led to a 60% reduction in smoking—without economic collapse. The same can be done with alcohol.
  • Alternative Industries: The jobs lost in brewing and distilling could be diversified into sectors producing non-alcoholic beverages, craft sodas, or even industries focused on addiction recovery and mental health.
  • Healthcare Savings: If alcohol were prohibited, the U.S. could save over $200 billion annually in alcohol-related healthcare costs (NIH, 2023). That money could fund education, infrastructure, and social services instead.

The real choice is between:

  • A legal industry that profits from addiction
  • A healthy society where people are not enslaved by corporations pushing poison

The former is economic practicality; the latter is moral responsibility.

2. Personal Choice vs. Public Harm: The Slippery Slope of Vice

The rallying cry of "My body, my choice" is often invoked against prohibition, but this argument crumbles under scrutiny:

  • No Right is Absolute: We ban other harmful substances (heroin, crack cocaine) not because users will die alone, but because their choices harm others—through crime, emergency room burdens, and broken families.
  • Secondhand Drunkenness: Unlike smoking (which can be confined to certain areas), alcohol’s harm extends to innocent victims—spouses, children, pedestrians killed by drunk drivers.
  • Historical Precedent: We have already made these choices as a society. We ban gambling addictions, prostitution, and public intoxication because they tear at the social fabric. Alcohol does the same—and worse.

If personal freedom is the only concern, then why do we have laws against public drunkenness, underage drinking, or drunk driving? If your "choice" to drink leads to you harming others, society has every right to intervene.

3. Enforcement in the 21st Century: Learning from Past Mistakes

Opponents point to the Prohibition era (1920–1933) and argue that it failed—leading to speakeasies, organized crime, and corruption. However, this critique ignores three critical differences between then and now:

  1. Modern Surveillance and Technology – Today, we have mass surveillance, AI-driven policing, and biometric tracking that make interdiction far more effective. Alcohol could be tracked through purchase histories, vehicle telematics, and mandatory sobriety checkpoints.
  2. Decriminalization of Addiction – Instead of jailing users (as happened in the 1920s), modern prohibition could focus on treatment courts, mandatory rehab, and harm reduction for those struggling with addiction.
  3. Global Examples of Success – Countries like Saudi Arabia and Iran maintain strict alcohol prohibition with low tolerance for black markets. Their approaches—not 1920s America’s flawed implementation—should serve as a model.

A gradual, well-regulated prohibition could avoid past mistakes by:

  • Phasing out alcohol sales over 5–10 years to allow businesses to transition.
  • Investing in addiction treatment programs to help those already dependent.
  • Cracking down on black markets with penalties far harsher than those for alcohol-related crimes today (e.g., mandatory minimum sentences for illegal distribution).

The 1920s failure was not in the principle of prohibition, but in weak enforcement and public opposition. Today, with increased awareness of addiction as a disease, a stronger moral consensus, and superior enforcement tools, prohibition could succeed where it once struggled.

A Call to Moral Action: Restore Temperance for a Greater America

The case for reinstating national prohibition is overwhelmingly clear:

  • Alcohol destroys public health, killing more Americans each year than opioid overdoses, car accidents, and guns combined.
  • It dismantles families, fuels domestic violence, and leaves children scarred for life.
  • It corrodes morality, turning communities into vice-ridden wastelands instead of bastions of virtue and industry.
  • The economic and libertarian objections crumble under scrutiny—history shows regulation works, freedom must have limits, and enforcement is far stronger today than in the 1920s.

Some will resist, arguing that America cannot change, that vices are inevitable, that we must accept the status quo. But history proves otherwise:

  • We ended slavery against enormous opposition.
  • We established women’s suffrage despite fierce backlash.
  • We banned lead in paint and gasoline, saving millions from permanent damage.

Moral progress is never easy—but it is always necessary. The time has come to reject the poison of legalized drunkenness and reclaim sobriety, discipline, and human dignity as core American values.

A Proposed Path Forward

To implement prohibition effectively, Congress should:

  1. Phase Out Legal Sales Over 5 Years – Gradually increase taxes, restrictions, and penalties while transitioning businesses to non-alcoholic products.
  2. Criminalize Production, Sale, and Public Consumption – With strict enforcement, mandatory rehabilitation for addicts, and heavy penalties for illegal distribution.
  3. Invest in Addiction Treatment and Recovery – Expand facilities, mental health programs, and social services to help those dependent on alcohol.
  4. Public Awareness Campaigns – Educate citizens on the dangers of alcohol and promote sobriety as a virtue.
  5. Support Workers in Transition – Provide tax incentives for breweries and bars to pivot to soda production, bottled water, or hospitality-alternative businesses.

This is not a pipe dream—it is a moral imperative that past generations understood, and today’s must embrace. America was not built on the backs of drunkards, but on the fortitude of sober, hardworking citizens. It is time to restore that foundation.

Conclusion: A Sober Future for a Stronger Nation

The question before us is simple: Do we value life and virtue, or do we surrender to vice and decay? For too long, America has chosen the latter—chasing fleeting pleasures while millions suffer, families break, and public health crumbles. The experiment of legalized alcohol has failed. The body count of alcohol-related deaths, the wreckage of broken homes, and the moral decline of a once-great nation demand bold, decisive action.

Reinstating prohibition is not about paternalism—it is about protection. Protecting the vulnerable from addiction. Protecting families from violence. Protecting society from preventable suffering. History has shown that when a nation prioritizes health over profit, virtue over vice, and the collective good over individual indulgence, greatness follows.

It is time to rid our land of this scourge. It is time to reclaim the promise of a sober, disciplined, and morally upright America. It is time for Prohibition 2.0—not as a temporary measure, but as a permanent reaffirmation of what it means to be a great and free people.

Let us not shrink from the challenge. Let us lead. Together, we can build an America untainted by alcohol’s poison—an America where health flourishes, families thrive, and morality prevails. The choice is ours. The hour is now. National prohibition must be reinstated.

The Case for Prohibition: A Call to Reclaim America's Health, Safety, and Moral Compass

Introduction

On January 16, 1919, the United States ratified the Eighteenth Amendment, enshrining into law a bold moral vision: that the nation would be better off without the scourge of alcohol. Though repealed just fourteen years later, the arguments that animated the Prohibition movement were not born of ignorance or fanaticism—they were rooted in observable, measurable, and devastating consequences of alcohol on American life. Over a century later, those consequences have not diminished. They have multiplied. Every year, alcohol kills more than 178,000 Americans, costs the economy hundreds of billions of dollars, tears families apart, fuels violence and crime, and burdens a healthcare system already stretched to its breaking point. The time has come to revisit the question our forebears had the courage to ask: Would America be better off without alcohol? The evidence—scientific, economic, and moral—overwhelmingly suggests that the answer is yes. The United States should reinstate a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages.

I. The Public Health Imperative

A. Alcohol Is One of the Leading Preventable Causes of Death

The scientific case against alcohol is no longer a matter of debate among researchers—it is a matter of consensus. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), excessive alcohol use is responsible for approximately 178,000 deaths per year in the United States, making it the third-leading preventable cause of death behind only tobacco and poor diet/physical inactivity. These are not abstract statistics. Each number represents a human life—a parent, a child, a friend—cut short by a substance that society has chosen to normalize.

The diseases attributable to alcohol are extensive and devastating: liver cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, pancreatitis, multiple forms of cancer (including breast, colon, liver, esophageal, and throat cancers), cardiovascular disease, stroke, and neurological damage. The World Health Organization has classified alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen—the same category as asbestos and tobacco—meaning there is sufficient evidence that it causes cancer in humans. No amount of alcohol consumption is considered entirely "safe." A landmark 2018 study published in The Lancet, analyzing data from 195 countries, concluded unequivocally: "The safest level of drinking is none."

If any other consumer product were introduced today and shown to cause this magnitude of harm, it would never receive regulatory approval. Imagine if a pharmaceutical company applied for approval of a drug that caused cancer, liver failure, brain damage, birth defects, and over 178,000 annual deaths. The application would be rejected immediately, and rightly so. Yet we continue to permit, regulate, and even celebrate the sale of such a substance—because it is culturally entrenched.

B. The Mental Health and Addiction Crisis

Approximately 29.5 million Americans aged 12 and older suffer from Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD), according to the 2022 National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Fewer than 10 percent receive treatment. Alcohol is, by a wide margin, the most widely used addictive substance in the country, and its addictive properties are systematically underestimated because of its cultural ubiquity.

Alcohol addiction destroys brain chemistry, impairs judgment, erodes impulse control, and creates a vicious cycle of dependency that is extraordinarily difficult to break. It is a leading contributor to depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation. Nearly one in five suicides in the United States involves alcohol. Among adolescents, early alcohol use is strongly correlated with the development of lifelong addiction patterns, impaired cognitive development, and reduced educational attainment.

A society that knowingly permits the widespread distribution of a substance this addictive—and then struggles to fund treatment for the millions who fall victim to it—is engaged in a form of collective self-harm. Prohibition would not eliminate addiction overnight, but it would dramatically reduce the flow of new victims into the pipeline.

C. The Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disaster

Alcohol is the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability in the United States. Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASDs) affect an estimated 1 to 5 percent of the population and result in lifelong cognitive, behavioral, and physical impairments. No amount of alcohol is safe during pregnancy, yet roughly 14 percent of pregnant women report drinking at some point during their pregnancy.

Every case of FASD represents a preventable tragedy—a child burdened with developmental challenges before drawing their first breath, not because of genetics or fate, but because a legal and socially normalized substance was available. A prohibition would send the clearest possible signal that the protection of unborn children is a paramount societal value and would materially reduce the incidence of these devastating conditions.

II. The Social and Public Safety Imperative

A. Alcohol and Violence

The relationship between alcohol and violence is one of the most robustly documented findings in all of criminology and public health research. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) reports that alcohol is involved in approximately 40 percent of violent crimes in the United States. Two-thirds of victims of intimate partner violence report that the perpetrator had been drinking. Approximately 40 percent of child abuse cases involve a parent with an alcohol problem. Alcohol is implicated in a significant proportion of homicides, sexual assaults, aggravated assaults, and domestic violence incidents.

Prohibition opponents often argue that people, not substances, commit violence. This is technically true but dangerously incomplete. Alcohol fundamentally alters brain function—it impairs the prefrontal cortex (responsible for judgment and impulse control), amplifies aggression, and distorts perception of social cues. It does not merely correlate with violence; it causally contributes to it. A policy that tolerates the free sale of a substance that predictably turns a measurable percentage of its users violent is, in effect, a policy that accepts a certain baseline level of preventable violence as the cost of doing business. We should refuse to pay that cost.

B. Alcohol and Automobile Fatalities

In 2022, 13,524 people were killed in alcohol-impaired driving crashes in the United States, accounting for roughly 32 percent of all traffic fatalities. This is the equivalent of a fully loaded commercial airplane crashing every week for an entire year—and yet it barely registers in the national consciousness because it happens one or two deaths at a time.

These are not accidents in any meaningful sense of the word. They are the predictable, preventable consequence of a policy choice. Every one of those 13,524 people—mothers driving home from work, children in back seats, teenagers on their way to school—died because our society decided that the pleasure of drinking was worth the certainty that some of our citizens would be killed by drunk drivers. Prohibition would not eliminate drunk driving entirely (some would obtain alcohol illegally), but it would reduce it dramatically—just as the original Prohibition era saw significant declines in alcohol-related hospital admissions, liver cirrhosis deaths, and arrests for public drunkenness.

C. Alcohol and Crime, Homelessness, and Poverty

Alcohol is a factor in a vast proportion of arrests, incarcerations, emergency room visits, and homeless shelter admissions. It is the substance most commonly associated with emergency department visits. It contributes to workplace accidents, lost productivity, and unemployment. The economic cost of excessive alcohol use in the United States is estimated at approximately $249 billion per year (2010 dollars), with a substantial portion borne by the public through healthcare costs, law enforcement, criminal justice, and social services.

These costs are not borne equally. They fall disproportionately on the poor, on communities of color, and on rural communities with limited access to treatment and recovery resources. In effect, the legal alcohol industry privatizes its profits while socializing its enormous costs—transferring the burden of alcohol's destruction onto taxpayers, families, and communities that can least afford it. This is not a free market at work; it is a subsidy for suffering.

III. The Moral Imperative

A. The Limits of Personal Liberty

The most common objection to prohibition is an appeal to personal liberty: "What I drink is my own business." This argument is philosophically appealing but practically indefensible, because alcohol's harms are almost never confined to the individual drinker.

The drunk driver who kills a pedestrian has made a choice for that pedestrian. The parent whose alcoholism traumatizes their children has made a choice for those children. The employer whose intoxicated employee causes a workplace accident has made a choice for that employee's coworkers. The taxpayer who funds the emergency room visits, the criminal justice proceedings, and the social services for alcohol-related harms has had a choice made for them. Alcohol is perhaps the most potent example of a substance whose consumption creates massive negative externalities—costs imposed on unwilling third parties by the choices of the user.

A mature, moral society recognizes that individual liberty does not extend to actions that impose severe and predictable harm on others. We already accept this principle in countless domains: we require seat belts, ban texting while driving, regulate pollution, and restrict the sale of other dangerous substances. Prohibition of alcohol is not a radical departure from this principle—it is a logical and overdue application of it.

B. The Moral Duty to Protect the Vulnerable

Every major moral tradition in human history—from Christianity to Islam to Buddhism to secular humanism—has recognized the dangers of intoxication. The biblical Book of Proverbs warns, "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Proverbs 20:1). The Quran explicitly prohibits alcohol (5:90). The Buddhist precepts discourage intoxication. These traditions, spanning millennia and cultures, converge on a single insight: substances that impair reason and judgment pose a profound threat to human flourishing.

A moral society has an obligation to protect its most vulnerable members: children, victims of domestic violence, individuals predisposed to addiction, the unborn, and those too young or too marginalized to advocate for themselves. The current policy of legal, regulated alcohol sale fails this obligation comprehensively. It makes alcohol available on virtually every street corner, markets it aggressively through billions of dollars in advertising (often targeting young people and communities of color), and then offers woefully inadequate treatment and support for those who fall victim to its effects.

C. The Question of What Kind of Society We Choose to Be

Ultimately, the question of prohibition is not merely a policy question—it is a question of national identity and values. What kind of society do we want to be?

Do we want to be a society that spends $249 billion a year cleaning up the wreckage of alcohol while telling ourselves there is no alternative? Do we want to be a society that buries 178,000 of its citizens every year from a preventable cause and calls it freedom? Do we want to be a society that allows corporations to profit enormously from the addiction of millions while underfunding treatment and prevention? Do we want to be a society that shrugs at 13,000 drunk driving deaths a year as the price of a Friday night?

Or do we want to be a society with the courage to say: enough? We can do better. We can build a culture of health, clarity, and mutual responsibility. We can choose a future in which the next generation does not inherit the same cycle of addiction, violence, and preventable death.

IV. Addressing Counterarguments

"Prohibition Didn't Work the First Time."

This is the most common objection, and it deserves a serious answer. The historical record of Prohibition is more nuanced than popular culture suggests. During Prohibition (1920–1933):

  • Alcohol consumption dropped by an estimated 30–50 percent.
  • Cirrhosis death rates declined by nearly 50 percent.
  • Hospital admissions for alcohol-related psychosis dropped dramatically.
  • Arrests for public drunkenness fell significantly.
  • Rates of absenteeism in industrial settings improved.

Prohibition was imperfect—particularly in its enforcement mechanisms and its inability to address demand-side factors—but it produced measurable public health benefits. Its repeal was driven more by political and economic factors (the onset of the Great Depression, the desire for tax revenue, and the lobbying of the alcohol industry) than by evidence that it had "failed."

Moreover, a reinstated prohibition would benefit from a century of advances in public health infrastructure, pharmacological understanding of addiction, treatment modalities, and regulatory capacity. We have tools today that the temperance movement could not have imagined: medication-assisted treatment, cognitive behavioral therapy, vast public health surveillance systems, and evidence-based prevention programs. A modern prohibition, implemented alongside robust investment in treatment, education, and alternative social activities, could succeed where the first effort fell short.

"People Will Just Get Alcohol Illegally."

Some will—just as some people use illegal drugs today. But this argument, taken to its logical conclusion, would require the legalization of every dangerous substance, including heroin, methamphetamine, and fentanyl. The fact that a law will not achieve perfect compliance is not an argument against having the law. Speed limit laws do not prevent all speeding, but they dramatically reduce the number of people who drive at dangerous speeds, and they save thousands of lives per year as a result. A prohibition on alcohol would similarly reduce consumption and its associated harms, even if it could not eliminate them entirely.

"The Alcohol Industry Employs Millions and Generates Tax Revenue."

This argument is morally bankrupt. The tobacco industry also employs millions and generates tax revenue. So did the slave economy. The economic benefits of an industry do not justify the human suffering it produces. Moreover, the economic costs of alcohol ($249 billion annually) vastly exceed the tax revenue it generates (approximately $15 billion in federal and state excise taxes). By any rational cost-benefit analysis, alcohol is an economic net loss for American society.

"People Should Be Free to Make Their Own Choices."

As discussed above, alcohol's harms are overwhelmingly externalized. But even setting aside the question of externalities, a compassionate society does not simply allow its citizens to destroy themselves with a substance that hijacks the brain's reward circuitry and progressively erodes the very capacity for autonomous decision-making. Freedom is not merely the absence of restriction—it is the capacity to live a life of health, dignity, and purpose. A substance that undermines that capacity for millions of Americans is not an instrument of freedom; it is an instrument of bondage.

V. A Vision for a Post-Alcohol America

A reinstated prohibition need not be punitive or puritanical. It could be accompanied by:

  • Massive investment in addiction treatment and recovery services, making evidence-based care available to every American who needs it, free of charge.
  • Public health campaigns that address the cultural normalization of alcohol and promote alternative forms of social connection, relaxation, and celebration.
  • Economic transition support for workers and communities currently dependent on the alcohol industry.
  • Research and development of non-alcoholic beverages and social spaces that replicate the communal benefits of bars and restaurants without the harm.
  • Gradual implementation with clear timelines, public education, and community engagement to ensure broad social buy-in.

The goal is not a joyless, austere society—it is a healthier, safer, and more just one.

Conclusion

The evidence is overwhelming. Alcohol is a leading cause of preventable death, a driver of violence and crime, a destroyer of families, a burden on public finances, and a barrier to human flourishing. The arguments for its continued legal availability rest on a distorted conception of personal liberty, a romanticized reading of Prohibition history, and the political influence of an industry that profits from human suffering.

The United States once had the moral courage to declare that this substance was incompatible with the health and welfare of its people. That judgment was correct then, and it is even more correct now—backed by a century of additional scientific evidence, public health data, and lived experience. We should not romanticize the past, but neither should we be prisoners of it. A modern prohibition, implemented with wisdom, compassion, and investment in human well-being, would save hundreds of thousands of lives, prevent immeasurable suffering, and move this nation closer to the ideals of justice, health, and genuine freedom to which it has always aspired.

The question is not whether we can afford to reinstate Prohibition. The question is whether we can afford not to.

A Necessary Return: The Case for Reinstating National Prohibition

The United States once undertook a bold experiment in public virtue. From 1920 to 1933, the Eighteenth Amendment banned the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors. Alcohol corporations spend billions each year on advertising designed to normalize consumption, target young adults, and cultivate lifelong customers. The reinstatement of national prohibition is not a regressive policy but a necessary step to protect public health, strengthen families, and restore moral integrity to society. The Unfinished Experiment: A Case for Reinstating National Prohibition

Why America Must Revisit Its Most Courageous Public Health Initiative

Introduction

On January 17, 1920, the United States embarked on what historian Herbert Asbury called "The Great Experiment"—the national prohibition of the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors under the Eighteenth Amendment. Thirteen years later, in the depths of the Great Depression, a weary nation repealed Prohibition under circumstances of economic desperation and organized political pressure from wealthy industrialists eager to restore their fortunes. In the nearly a century since repeal, American society has treated Prohibition as a punchline—a naïve, puritanical overreach that "didn't work." This lazy consensus has gone virtually unchallenged, even as alcohol has quietly become one of the most destructive forces in American life, killing more citizens annually than opioids, disfiguring millions of families, and draining hundreds of billions of dollars from the economy. The dismissal of Prohibition is not grounded in evidence; it is grounded in cultural mythology carefully cultivated by one of the most powerful and profitable industries on earth.

The time has come for an honest, evidence-based reassessment. When we examine the exposed nerves of American public health—the staggering death tolls, the epidemic of alcohol-related violence, the shattered families, and the targeted exploitation of vulnerable communities—the moral and practical case for reinstating a national prohibition on alcoholic beverages is not merely plausible. It is overwhelming.

I. The Scale of the Catastrophe: Alcohol as America's Quiet Plague

The first obstacle to clear thinking about alcohol policy is the systematic normalization of alcohol's devastation. Because drinking is culturally ubiquitous, its consequences are rendered invisible—diffused across emergency rooms, morgues, courtrooms, foster care agencies, and psychiatric wards where they are counted under dozens of other categories. When assembled into a single portrait, the picture is staggering.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, excessive alcohol use kills approximately 178,000 Americans every year, making it the fourth leading preventable cause of death in the United States. To place that figure in context, this is roughly equivalent to a fully loaded Boeing 737 crashing every single day with no survivors—an unthinkable catastrophe that, if it involved aviation, would ground every plane in the country within hours. Yet because these deaths arrive one at a time—a cirrhotic liver here, a drunk-driving fatality there, an alcohol-poisoning death in a college dormitory elsewhere—they provoke no national alarm.

These 178,000 annual deaths are not an abstraction. They represent mothers, fathers, children, veterans, and neighbors. They include approximately 13,000 drunk-driving fatalities per year, tens of thousands of deaths from alcoholic liver disease, alcohol-related cancers (the World Health Organization has classified alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen, in the same category as asbestos and tobacco), and thousands of fatalities from acute alcohol poisoning. They include the uncounted victims of alcohol-fueled homicides, suicides, and domestic violence incidents.

Beyond mortality, the morbidity figures are equally catastrophic. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism estimates that approximately 29.5 million Americans meet the diagnostic criteria for Alcohol Use Disorder in any given year. Nearly 100,000 sexual assaults annually involve alcohol. Alcohol is implicated in roughly 40 percent of all violent crimes and is present in approximately half of all domestic violence incidents. The economic cost, encompassing healthcare expenditures, lost productivity, criminal justice expenses, and property damage, exceeds $249 billion annually—a figure that dwarfs the tax revenue generated by alcohol sales, which amounts to roughly $10 billion at the federal level.

No other consumer product in America produces carnage at this scale while remaining freely available at corner stores, gas stations, and grocery checkout lanes. If any other substance or product killed 178,000 Americans a year, triggered nearly 30 million cases of clinical addiction, and cost a quarter-trillion dollars annually, the public outcry for prohibition would be deafening. The only reason alcohol escapes this scrutiny is cultural inertia and the political power of the alcohol industry. Neither constitutes a moral argument.

II. The Historical Record: Prohibition Worked Far Better Than We Admit

The most common objection to prohibition is the confident assertion that "it didn't work." This claim has been repeated so frequently and so uncritically that it has achieved the status of received wisdom. It is, nevertheless, substantially false.

The serious historical and epidemiological evidence tells a far more nuanced story—one that, on balance, strongly supports the effectiveness of national Prohibition as a public health measure.

Alcohol consumption plummeted. During Prohibition, per capita alcohol consumption declined by an estimated 60 to 70 percent from pre-Prohibition levels, according to economists Jeffrey Miron and Jeffrey Zwiebel as well as research published in the American Journal of Public Health. Even at its highest point during the later years of Prohibition, consumption never returned to pre-1920 levels. This decline was not marginal; it was dramatic, and it had measurable consequences.

Cirrhosis deaths dropped sharply. Deaths from liver cirrhosis, the most reliable long-term biomarker of heavy alcohol consumption, fell by approximately 50 percent during Prohibition. This decline was observable almost immediately upon enactment and persisted throughout the Prohibition period. After repeal, cirrhosis rates began climbing again and eventually surpassed pre-Prohibition levels—a pattern that, by itself, constitutes powerful evidence that Prohibition saved tens of thousands of lives.

Alcohol-related hospital admissions declined. Admissions to state hospitals for alcoholic psychosis dropped by more than 60 percent in several states during the early years of Prohibition. Public drunkenness arrests also fell dramatically.

Domestic violence and family stability improved. While comprehensive statistics from this era are limited, contemporary accounts and social work records indicate significant reductions in domestic violence and family abandonment during Prohibition. The saloon—which had been the epicenter of male drinking culture and a major contributor to family poverty—effectively ceased to exist. Savings rates among working-class families increased.

The "crime wave" narrative is exaggerated. The most persistent critique of Prohibition centers on organized crime. There is no denying that Prohibition created black markets and empowered criminal syndicates. However, several correctives are in order. First, organized crime in America predated Prohibition and persisted long after repeal; the Mafia continued to thrive for decades on gambling, narcotics, extortion, and labor racketeering. Second, the violence associated with Prohibition-era bootlegging was overwhelmingly concentrated among criminals killing other criminals in territorial disputes—not random violence against the public. Third, and most importantly, the comparison must be made not between Prohibition and some crime-free utopia, but between the harms of black-market alcohol and the vastly larger harms of legal, freely available alcohol. The approximately 400 gangland murders per year during Prohibition pale beside the 178,000 annual alcohol-related deaths we accept today as simply the cost of doing business.

The notion that Prohibition "failed" is, in essence, a narrative constructed largely by the Association Against the Prohibition Amendment—a lobbying group funded by wealthy industrialists like the du Pont family, who sought repeal partly because they wanted alcohol tax revenue to replace income taxes on the wealthy. This origin should give us pause. The "failure" narrative serves the interests of the alcohol industry and wealthy elites; it does not accurately reflect the public health evidence.

III. The Moral Dimension: A Society's Obligation to Protect the Vulnerable

Beyond the empirical data, the case for prohibition carries a profound moral weight that a civilized society cannot in good conscience ignore.

Alcohol preys on the vulnerable. The alcohol industry does not survive on moderate, occasional drinkers. Research consistently shows that the heaviest 10 percent of drinkers account for the majority of all alcohol consumed. The industry's business model depends upon addiction, heavy use, and the exploitation of those least able to exercise free choice in the matter—including adolescents, individuals with genetic predispositions to addiction, people suffering from mental illness, and economically marginalized communities deliberately targeted by predatory marketing.

The concept of "individual choice" that undergirds opposition to prohibition is philosophically incoherent when applied to a substance that, by its very pharmacological nature, compromises the capacity for rational choice. Alcohol is a powerful psychoactive drug that impairs judgment, reduces impulse control, fosters physical dependence, and restructures neural reward pathways. To speak of an alcoholic "choosing" to drink is akin to speaking of a drowning person "choosing" to gasp for air. The libertarian framework of autonomous consumer choice collapses when the product in question chemically undermines the autonomy on which that framework depends.

The harm is not confined to the user. Unlike many personal lifestyle choices, alcohol consumption generates enormous externalities—harms imposed upon non-consenting third parties. The child physically abused by a drunken parent did not choose to drink. The family killed by a drunk driver did not choose to drink. The woman sexually assaulted at a party did not choose to drink. The taxpayer funding $249 billion in alcohol-related costs did not choose to drink. The fetus permanently brain-damaged by prenatal alcohol exposure did not choose to drink. A coherent commitment to individual liberty must include the liberty of innocent people not to be harmed by others' intoxication, and that liberty is massively violated under the current regime.

Children deserve special moral consideration. Approximately 10 percent of American children—more than 7 million—live with at least one parent who has an alcohol use disorder. These children experience higher rates of abuse, neglect, poverty, academic failure, emotional trauma, and subsequent addiction. The intergenerational transmission of alcohol-related damage represents one of the most profound moral failures of American society. A nation that professes to care about children while making their primary destroyer available on every block is engaged in a form of collective moral hypocrisy that demands confrontation.

The alcohol industry is morally bankrupt. The modern alcohol industry spends approximately $7 to $8 billion annually on advertising and marketing in the United States, much of it designed—despite pro forma disclaimers—to appeal to young people, to associate drinking with attractiveness, success, athletic prowess, and social belonging, and to normalize heavy consumption. Industry-funded "responsibility" campaigns are demonstrably designed to be ineffective, serving as public relations shields rather than genuine harm-reduction efforts. An industry that profits from addiction and death, that lobbies against every meaningful regulation, and that targets vulnerable populations with precision marketing has forfeited any claim to moral legitimacy.

IV. Addressing Objections: Why the Standard Arguments Against Prohibition Fail

Opponents of prohibition advance several objections that, while superficially appealing, do not withstand rigorous scrutiny.

"You can't legislate morality." This is perhaps the most vacuous objection in American political discourse. Every law legislates morality. Laws against murder, theft, fraud, child abuse, and environmental pollution all reflect moral judgments about what constitutes acceptable conduct. The question is never whether to legislate morality, but which moral principles deserve legal enforcement. The principle that society should not permit the commercial sale of a product that kills 178,000 of its citizens annually is at least as defensible as the principle that society should not permit the commercial sale of, say, lawn darts (banned in 1988 after killing three children).

"Prohibition creates black markets." This is true, and the challenge is real. However, several points weaken this objection considerably. First, as noted above, the black-market harms of Prohibition were far smaller than the harms of legal alcohol today. We are essentially arguing that we must tolerate 178,000 deaths per year to avoid the lesser harms of black-market activity. Second, modern law enforcement possesses surveillance, forensic, and intelligence capabilities unimaginable in 1920—making effective enforcement far more feasible. Third, the black-market objection, if taken seriously, would require legalizing every dangerous substance, including methamphetamine, heroin, and fentanyl, since their prohibition also creates black markets. The fact that virtually no one advocates this position reveals that the black-market argument is applied selectively to alcohol, not as a matter of principle.

"People have a right to drink." No such right exists in the Constitution, in natural law theory, or in any serious philosophical framework. The Declaration of Independence speaks of rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Alcohol systematically destroys all three—not only for drinkers but for millions of innocent bystanders. If anything, the inalienable rights articulated in our founding documents argue for prohibition, since the right to life of the drunk-driving victim surely supersedes the right of the driver to purchase a six-pack.

"Moderate drinking is harmless—even beneficial." The long-promoted claim that moderate alcohol consumption provides cardiovascular benefits has been substantially debunked. A landmark 2018 study published in The Lancet, analyzing data from 195 countries, concluded unequivocally that "the safest level of drinking is none." Subsequent research, including a comprehensive 2022 analysis in JAMA Network Open, confirmed that previously observed "benefits" of moderate drinking were artifacts of methodological flaws—specifically, the inclusion of former heavy drinkers and people with preexisting illness in "abstainer" control groups. The scientific consensus has shifted decisively: there is no safe level of alcohol consumption. This removes the last empirical pillar supporting the notion that legal alcohol serves any public health interest whatsoever.

"It's a matter of personal freedom." Personal freedom is a vital value, but it has never been understood—by any serious political philosopher from Locke to Mill to Rawls—as absolute and unlimited. John Stuart Mill himself, the patron saint of individual liberty, articulated the "harm principle": that individual freedom may legitimately be restricted to prevent harm to others. Given that alcohol generates more third-party harm than virtually any other consumer product in existence, Mill's own framework provides robust justification for prohibition. The "freedom" argument also conveniently ignores the millions of Americans trapped in addiction who have effectively lost their freedom to alcohol and who might never have become addicted had the substance not been commercially available and relentlessly marketed.

V. A Modern Prohibition: Practical Considerations for the Twenty-First Century

A renewed prohibition need not replicate every feature of the 1920-1933 experiment. A modern prohibition could incorporate lessons learned, advances in technology, and more sophisticated implementation strategies.

Phased implementation. Rather than an abrupt ban, a modern prohibition could proceed in stages: first eliminating advertising and marketing, then progressively restricting points of sale, increasing taxes to reduce demand, lowering legal alcohol content thresholds, and ultimately achieving full prohibition over a period of five to ten years. This graduated approach would allow for adjustment and would reduce the shock to the economy and the incentive for immediate black-market development.

Comprehensive treatment infrastructure. A portion of the $249 billion currently lost to alcohol-related costs could be redirected toward building a world-class addiction treatment and recovery infrastructure—ensuring that the millions of Americans currently dependent on alcohol receive the medical and psychological support necessary for recovery. Unlike in 1920, we now possess evidence-based pharmacological and behavioral treatments for alcohol dependence.

Investment in enforcement technology. Modern surveillance, data analytics, financial tracking, and forensic capabilities make enforcement vastly more feasible than it was a century ago. International cooperation frameworks developed for narcotics enforcement could be adapted to alcohol. The illicit production of distilled spirits, in particular, is substantially more difficult to conceal than the cultivation of plants.

Community and cultural investment. Prohibition should be accompanied by massive investment in community institutions, recreational facilities, mental health services, and social support systems that address the underlying conditions—loneliness, despair, trauma, boredom—that drive people to drink. The saloon filled a social void in American life; a responsible society must fill that void with healthier alternatives.

Constitutional pathway. As an amendment repealed the Eighteenth Amendment, so an amendment could repeal the Twenty-First. The constitutional framework for prohibition already exists and has been tested. The political difficulty of achieving such an amendment is real but is not an argument against the moral rightness of the goal.

VI. The Precedent of Tobacco: Proof That Cultural Denormalization Works

Skeptics who insist that American culture will never accept prohibition should consider the extraordinary transformation of attitudes toward tobacco. In 1960, approximately 42 percent of American adults smoked cigarettes. Smoking was ubiquitous in offices, restaurants, airplanes, hospitals, and even doctors' offices. The tobacco industry was politically untouchable. The idea that smoking could be banned in virtually all public places, that cigarette advertising could be eliminated from television, that smoking rates could be cut by more than two-thirds, would have seemed as fantastical as the idea of alcohol prohibition seems today.

Yet it happened—through a combination of public health education, advertising restrictions, taxation, litigation, and progressive regulation. Today, smoking is socially stigmatized to a degree that would have been unimaginable two generations ago. The public health results have been extraordinary: lung cancer rates have fallen dramatically, cardiovascular disease has declined, and millions of lives have been saved.

Alcohol is following a remarkably similar trajectory, albeit several decades behind. Public awareness of alcohol's harms is growing. The "sober curious" movement is gaining cultural momentum, particularly among younger Americans. Studies show that Generation Z drinks significantly less than previous generations. The scientific consensus on alcohol's harms has hardened. The cultural conditions for a fundamental reassessment of alcohol policy are emerging. Prohibition, far from being a relic of a bygone era, may represent the logical culmination of a public health revolution already underway.

VII. A Moral Imperative for Our Time

Ultimately, the question of prohibition is not a question of policy optimization or economic efficiency, though it passes both tests. It is a question of moral seriousness.

Do we, as a society, accept that 178,000 of our neighbors will die needlessly every year so that the rest of us may enjoy a glass of wine with dinner? Do we accept that nearly 30 million of our fellow citizens will be imprisoned by chemical addiction so that a handful of corporations may profit? Do we accept that millions of children will grow up in homes poisoned by alcohol so that we may preserve an abstract notion of "personal freedom" that the addicted themselves do not experience? Do we accept that tens of thousands of women will be sexually assaulted, that thousands of innocent motorists will be killed, that our emergency rooms and prisons will overflow with alcohol's wreckage—all because we lack the collective courage to confront a cultural mythology manufactured by an industry that profits from human destruction?

The original prohibitionists—many of them women who had seen their families destroyed by alcohol, many of them African Americans seeking to protect their communities from predatory saloons, many of them labor activists fighting for the welfare of working-class families—were not naïve or puritanical. They were moral visionaries who recognized a catastrophe and had the courage to demand its end. History has treated them with contempt largely because the industries they challenged have written the history.

It is time to write a different chapter.

Conclusion

The evidence is unambiguous. Alcohol is the most destructive psychoactive substance in American society, killing more people than any illicit drug, tearing apart more families than any social pathology, and costing more than any other public health crisis short of the COVID-19 pandemic. The original Prohibition, far from the failure of popular mythology, produced dramatic improvements in public health outcomes that reversed upon repeal. The moral case for protecting vulnerable citizens—children, addiction-prone individuals, victims of alcohol-fueled violence—from a deliberately addictive and relentlessly marketed poison is as urgent today as it was in 1920.

A twenty-first-century prohibition, implemented wisely, phased gradually, supported by modern treatment and enforcement infrastructure, and accompanied by cultural investment in healthier communities, would save tens of thousands of lives every year, liberate millions from addiction, protect countless children from abuse and neglect, and reclaim hundreds of billions of dollars for productive use. It would represent not an infringement on freedom, but an expansion of it—freeing Americans from the tyranny of a substance that has held this nation hostage for far too long.

The Great Experiment was not a failure. It was abandoned. And every year, 178,000 Americans pay for that abandonment with their lives.

It is time to try again.

A Call for a Sober Nation

A Speech Advocating for National Prohibition

My fellow citizens,

I stand before you today with a heavy heart — but an unwavering conviction. I am here to speak a truth that too many are afraid to speak, a truth buried beneath billions of dollars of advertising, beneath cultural normalization, beneath the comforting lie that we have this problem "under control."

We do not have it under control.

Every single year in this nation, alcohol kills approximately 178,000 of our neighbors, our parents, our children, our friends. Let that number settle in your minds. One hundred and seventy-eight thousand. That is not a statistic. That is a graveyard. That is a city of empty chairs at dinner tables. That is a generation of children who will never know a parent's embrace.

If any other product — any pharmaceutical, any food, any consumer good — killed 178,000 Americans annually, we would not hesitate. We would not debate. We would not shrug our shoulders and say, "Well, people should just use it responsibly." We would act. We would protect our people. And yet, because the poison comes in a bottle with a clever label and a Super Bowl commercial, we look the other way.

Today, I am asking you to stop looking the other way.

I am calling for the return of national prohibition.

I. The Public Health Crisis We Refuse to Name

Let me lay the facts before you — not opinions, not moralizing, but facts.

Alcohol is the third leading preventable cause of death in the United States. It is a Group 1 carcinogen — classified by the World Health Organization in the same category as asbestos, tobacco smoke, and plutonium. It causes cancer of the liver, breast, colon, mouth, throat, and esophagus. Recent research from The Lancet has confirmed what many scientists have long suspected: there is no safe level of alcohol consumption. None. Zero.

We banned flavored cigarettes to protect children. We regulate trans fats. We pulled products off shelves for far lesser dangers. Yet we allow a proven carcinogen to be sold on every street corner in America, marketed with images of beauty, success, and celebration.

Alcohol is implicated in nearly half of all liver disease deaths. It is a leading contributor to heart disease, stroke, pancreatitis, and immune system dysfunction. It damages the developing brain — and let us be honest with ourselves: the developing brain does not stop developing at 21. It continues into the mid-twenties, and yet we hand young people a substance that is literally neurotoxic and tell them, "Welcome to adulthood."

We spend over $250 billion a year on the costs associated with excessive alcohol use — in healthcare, in lost productivity, in criminal justice, in shattered families. A quarter of a trillion dollars. Imagine what we could do with that money. Imagine the schools we could build. The treatment centers we could fund. The communities we could lift out of poverty.

And yet the alcohol industry generates roughly $250 billion in revenue, and they spend billions more ensuring that no politician, no regulator, no public health official dares to speak the words I am speaking today.

I dare.

II. The Toll on Our Families and Communities

But this is not only about statistics and dollars. This is about the fabric of our society — the thing that holds us together.

Walk into any family court in America on any given Monday morning. What will you find? You will find custody battles fueled by alcoholism. You will find children removed from homes because a parent could not put down the bottle. You will find domestic violence — because alcohol is involved in nearly 40% of violent crimes in this country. Forty percent.

Every 52 minutes, someone dies in an alcohol-impaired driving crash. Every. Fifty-two. Minutes. That is a classroom of people, gone, every single day, because we as a society have decided that the right to drink is more sacred than the right to come home alive.

Go to our emergency rooms on a Friday night. Talk to the nurses. Talk to the trauma surgeons. Ask them what they see. They will tell you about the young woman who came in with a shattered face because her partner had been drinking. They will tell you about the teenager pulled from a wreck, dead on arrival, a blood alcohol level three times the legal limit. They will tell you about the father who fell down the stairs, the mother who mixed her medications with wine, the college freshman who never woke up from a night of hazing.

And what do we say? "Drink responsibly."

What a cowardly phrase. What an abdication of our collective responsibility. We hand people an addictive, neurotoxic, carcinogenic substance and then blame them when they cannot control it. We know — the science tells us clearly — that approximately 10 to 15% of everyone who drinks will develop an alcohol use disorder. That is not a moral failing. That is pharmacology. That is the predictable result of exposing a population to an addictive drug.

We do not tell people to "use heroin responsibly." We do not tell people to "smoke methamphetamine in moderation." And yet alcohol, which kills more people than every illegal drug combined, gets a pass — because it is traditional, because it is cultural, because it is ours.

Since when has tradition been an excuse for destruction?

III. The Moral Question

Now, I know that some of you are uncomfortable when I use the word "moral." We live in a time when moral language has become unfashionable, when the assertion of any moral standard is treated as judgmental or intolerant.

But I ask you: Is it not a moral question when children go hungry because a parent spends their paycheck at a bar? Is it not a moral question when a woman is beaten by a man emboldened by liquor? Is it not a moral question when we, as a society, knowingly permit an industry to profit from addiction, suffering, and death?

Every great moral advance in this nation's history required someone to stand up and say: This is wrong, and we will no longer tolerate it.

We said it about the slave trade — an industry that was enormously profitable, deeply traditional, and fiercely defended by those who benefited from it. We said it about child labor. We said it about the unregulated sale of dangerous drugs. We said it, eventually, about tobacco — though not before millions had died.

The alcohol industry is the tobacco industry of our time. And history will judge us by how long we took to see it.

I believe that a good society protects its vulnerable. I believe that a good society does not allow corporate profits to outweigh human lives. I believe that a good society has the courage to look at the evidence, to count the dead, and to act — even when the action is unpopular, even when it is hard, even when it disrupts the comfortable habits of the privileged.

IV. Answering the Objections

Now, I am not naive. I know what you are thinking, because I have heard every objection a hundred times.

"Prohibition was tried and it failed."

Was it a failure? Let us look at the actual history, not the Hollywood version.

During Prohibition, cirrhosis deaths fell by nearly 50%. Admissions to mental hospitals for alcohol psychosis dropped dramatically. Alcohol-related arrests declined. Public drunkenness plummeted. Worker productivity rose. Exposed to it less, a generation of Americans drank less — and even after repeal, per capita alcohol consumption did not return to pre-Prohibition levels for nearly forty years.

Yes, there were speakeasies. Yes, there was organized crime. But organized crime existed before Prohibition and thrived long after it. The narrative that Prohibition single-handedly created the American mob is a myth — a myth propagated by the very industries that wanted repeal.

And let us be honest about why Prohibition was repealed. It was not repealed because the American people concluded it had failed. It was repealed because the Great Depression created an urgent need for tax revenue and jobs, and the alcohol industry lobbied relentlessly, spending enormous sums to convince Americans that repeal was the answer to their economic woes.

Sound familiar? The alcohol industry still uses economic arguments today. "Think of the jobs," they say. "Think of the tax revenue." As if there is no economic cost to 178,000 deaths a year. As if the quarter-trillion dollars we spend cleaning up alcohol's wreckage simply does not exist.

Moreover, we live in a fundamentally different world than 1920. We have modern law enforcement capabilities, digital surveillance tools, sophisticated border control, and — most importantly — we have nearly a century of experience in regulating controlled substances. We know what works. We know how to construct a modern prohibition that learns from the mistakes of the past.

"You can't legislate morality."

Every law legislates morality. Every single one. Laws against murder legislate morality. Laws against theft legislate morality. Speed limits, environmental regulations, child protection statutes — all of them represent society's moral judgment that certain behaviors cause unacceptable harm and must be prohibited.

The question is not whether we legislate morality. The question is which moral values we choose to protect. I am arguing that we should protect the value of human life over the value of human indulgence.

"What about personal freedom?"

I cherish personal freedom. But freedom has never meant the unrestricted right to harm yourself and others. You are not free to drive 120 miles per hour through a school zone. You are not free to fire a gun randomly into a crowd. You are not free to dump toxic waste into a river.

Your right to drink ends where another person's right to safety begins. And alcohol does not stay in the glass of the person who drinks it. It spills over — into our hospitals, onto our highways, into our homes, into the bruised faces of spouses and the frightened eyes of children.

John Stuart Mill himself — the great philosopher of liberty — argued that the state may restrict individual freedom to prevent harm to others. Alcohol causes more harm to others than nearly any other legal product in existence.

"People will just drink anyway."

People commit murder despite laws against it. People steal despite laws against theft. We do not therefore conclude that laws against murder and theft are pointless. The purpose of law is not to achieve perfect compliance. The purpose of law is to establish a social standard, to reduce harm, and to remove the institutional machinery that promotes and profits from destruction.

We do not need to catch every last person with a hidden bottle. We need to close the distilleries, shut down the breweries, end the advertising, remove the product from our shelves and our restaurants and our stadiums. We need to dismantle the infrastructure of addiction that currently operates with the full blessing of our government.

V. A Vision for a Sober Nation

Close your eyes for a moment and imagine it.

Imagine an America where emergency rooms on Saturday night are quiet. Where trauma surgeons have time to sit down. Where the leading cause of death for young people is no longer a preventable, alcohol-fueled tragedy.

Imagine neighborhoods where every dollar currently spent at a liquor store flows instead into grocery stores, into bookshops, into savings accounts, into college funds.

Imagine a nation where domestic violence rates are cut by a third. Where child protective services caseloads are halved. Where the foster care system is no longer overflowing with children whose only crime was being born to a parent who was sold a poison disguised as pleasure.

Imagine workplaces where Monday mornings are productive; where absenteeism drops, where workplace accidents decline, where the hidden costs of a drinking culture no longer drain our economy of hundreds of billions of dollars every year.

Imagine a culture that no longer tells its young people that adulthood begins with a drink. That celebrations require intoxication. That grief is best handled with a bottle. Imagine raising a generation of children who never see a beer commercial during a football game, who never associate alcohol with glamour, who grow up believing — because it is true — that joy and connection and courage are available to them without chemical assistance.

This is not a fantasy. This is a choice. And it is a choice that previous generations of Americans had the courage to make.

VI. A Call to Courage

I will not pretend this will be easy. The forces arrayed against this cause are enormous. The alcohol industry is one of the most powerful lobbying forces in Washington. They fund campaigns. They sponsor charities. They wrap themselves in the flag and in the language of freedom while poisoning the nation they claim to love.

Politicians will call this proposal extreme. Commentators will mock it. The industry will spend millions — billions — to make sure it never happens.

But I ask you: Who profits from the status quo?

Not the mother grieving her son, killed by a drunk driver. Not the child hiding in a closet while his father rages downstairs. Not the woman dying of breast cancer she might never have developed. Not the veteran self-medicating his trauma until it kills him. Not the Native communities devastated by a substance that was, let us remember, deliberately introduced as a tool of cultural destruction. Not the Black and Brown neighborhoods targeted with liquor store after liquor store, a practice so predatory it should shame us all.

The people who profit are shareholders and executives. Lobbyists and advertisers. The architects of addiction.

It is time to choose. Are we a nation that serves its people, or a nation that serves its industries? Are we a nation of courage, or a nation of convenience? Are we willing to endure the discomfort of change in order to save hundreds of thousands of lives?

VII. Conclusion

I began by telling you that 178,000 Americans die each year from alcohol. By the time I finish this speech, statistically, another person will have died. While we debate, while we deliberate, while we demur — they die.

Every great injustice persists because good people convince themselves that it is too big to fight, too entrenched to change, too normal to question.

Slavery was normal. Child labor was normal. Asbestos in our walls was normal. Cigarettes in hospitals were normal.

One day — and I believe this with every fiber of my being — one day, future generations will look back at this era and ask: How did they allow it? How did they let an industry sell poison to their own people and call it culture? How did they count 178,000 dead every year and call it freedom?

Let us be the generation that answers: We stopped it.

Let us be the generation with the moral clarity to see the truth, and the moral courage to act on it.

Let us bring about a new era of national prohibition — not out of prudishness, not out of puritanism, but out of love. Love for our neighbors. Love for our children. Love for the nation we want to become.

The bottle has had its say for long enough.

It is time for the people to speak.

Thank you.

Introduction
The United States has long grappled with the societal toll of alcohol consumption. While the 18th Amendment’s Prohibition (1920–1933) is often dismissed as a failed experiment, modern realities—escalating public health crises, entrenched moral challenges, and advancements in governance—demand a reevaluation. Reinstating a national prohibition on the sale and consumption of alcohol is not a step backward but a courageous, forward-thinking measure to safeguard public health and reaffirm our collective moral responsibility. Alcohol is a leading cause of preventable death in the U.S., claiming approximately 95,000 lives annually between 2016 and 2019, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This staggering toll surpasses deaths from opioids, automobile accidents, or gun violence. Chronic conditions like liver disease, cancer, and cardiovascular problems are disproportionately linked to alcohol, with the World Health Organization (WHO) attributing 1 in 7 deaths among adults aged 20–64 to alcohol use.

Economically, the CDC estimates alcohol’s annual burden at $250 billion, encompassing healthcare costs, lost productivity, and criminal justice expenditures. These figures do not account for the immeasurable suffering of families devastated by addiction, drunk-driving fatalities, or alcohol-induced mental health crises. Compare this to the success of smoking restrictions: after decades of regulation, smoking rates have plummeted, demonstrating that societal norms can shift when public health is prioritized. A prohibition would accelerate similar progress, reducing long-term healthcare burdens and reallocating resources to preventive care and treatment.

Moral Imperatives: Reshaping a Fractured Society

In homes where alcohol abuse is present, children face higher risks of neglect and trauma, perpetuating cycles of poverty and instability. By glamorizing intoxication, our current culture undermines values of responsibility, self-discipline, and community welfare.

Prohibition would signal a societal commitment to higher moral standards. Ethically, a society that prioritizes the vulnerable embodies a profound moral imperative.

Others contend that regulation, not prohibition, is the solution. A complete ban, paired with robust education and rehabilitation programs, would eliminate the root cause more effectively than half-measures.

Conclusion
Reinstating Prohibition is not about moralizing or denying personal autonomy; it is about confronting a crises that transcends individual choices. Alcohol’s catastrophic health impacts and corrosive influence on morality demand decisive action. By learning from past failures and leveraging modern advancements, the U.S. can build a society that values health, safety, and moral integrity. Let us prioritize the well-being of future generations over the interests of an industry that profits from suffering. The time has come to reclaim our collective future—one that is sober, united, and unburdened by the weight of alcohol’s devastation.
